items.q: What does an inverted index actually store?

options.t: Term → sorted list of the docs containing it
options.why: That's the whole idea: term to posting list. Instead of document to words, you store word to documents, so search becomes fetching a couple of short lists instead of reading everything.

options.t: For each document, the list of terms it contains
options.why: That's the forward index, which is what you already have — and it forces you to scan every document to answer a query. Inverting it is the entire point.

options.t: A B-tree over the text column
options.why: A B-tree answers 'starts with' but never 'contains', which is exactly why LIKE '%x%' degrades to a full scan on 500M rows.

options.t: A compressed copy of every document, sorted by relevance
options.why: Relevance depends on the query, so nothing can be pre-sorted by it. The index stores term-to-document mappings; ranking happens at query time.

items.q: Why are doc IDs in a posting list kept in ascending order?

options.t: So results come back in the right ranking order
options.why: Doc ID order has nothing to do with relevance order. Ranking is computed by the scorer after matching.

options.t: Intersection becomes a one-pass merge, and gaps compress
options.why: Two wins from one property. Sorted lists intersect in a single pass, and storing the gaps (12, 7, 8, ...) gives you small numbers that pack into a byte or two — which is how 50 billion postings fit in 250 GB and stay in cache.

options.t: Because Lucene requires documents to be inserted in ID order
options.why: Documents arrive in any order; the engine assigns and orders internal IDs itself. The sortedness is a design choice for speed and compression.

options.t: It keeps deletes cheap
options.why: Deletes are cheap because of tombstone bitmaps, not ordering. Ordering buys intersection speed and compression.

items.q: What is a skip pointer in a posting list?

options.t: A checkpoint every N entries, with a byte offset
options.why: Right — the express-train stops. When you ask 'is doc 4,410 in this list', you hop across checkpoints until you overshoot, then scan one small block, instead of walking millions of entries.

options.t: A pointer to the next segment holding the same term
options.why: Segments are separate indexes consulted independently. Skip pointers work inside one posting list.

options.t: A cached result for a previously seen query
options.why: That's a query cache, a different layer entirely. Skips are structural data inside the posting list itself.

options.t: A bloom filter that says whether a term exists
options.why: Bloom filters answer membership approximately; skip pointers accelerate exact seeks within a list you already found.

items.q: Compared with raw term counts, what do BM25's two main adjustments do?

options.t: Saturate repeats and normalize for length
options.why: Exactly. The 60th mention of 'waterproof' adds almost nothing, and a 4,000-word page shouldn't beat a tight 30-word listing just by being long. Those two fixes are the whole argument for BM25.

options.t: Boost newer documents and penalize old ones
options.why: Freshness is a ranking feature you may add yourself, but it isn't part of BM25 — BM25 only looks at term statistics and lengths.

options.t: Remove stopwords and apply stemming
options.why: Those are analyzer steps that run before scoring. BM25 operates on whatever terms the analyzer produced.

options.t: Weight documents by click-through rate
options.why: Behavioral signals belong to the phase-2 reranker. BM25 knows nothing about users.

items.q: In the query 'gore-tex boots', which term contributes more to the score, and why?

options.t: 'boots', because it appears in more documents
options.why: Backwards. Appearing everywhere makes a term uninformative — it barely narrows anything down.

options.t: They contribute equally; BM25 treats query terms symmetrically
options.why: BM25 weights every term by its IDF, so rare and common terms are treated very differently.

options.t: 'gore-tex', because it is rare across the corpus
options.why: Inverse document frequency: a term in 5,000 listings discriminates far better than one in 8 million. That's also why you drive the intersection from the rare term — cheap and correct agree.

options.t: Whichever appears first in the query
options.why: Position in the query text has no effect on bag-of-words scoring. Only phrase matching cares about order.

items.q: What is a segment in a Lucene-based search engine?

options.t: A small immutable index file made at each refresh
options.why: Yes. The in-memory buffer is frozen into a brand-new mini-index once per refresh interval, never edited afterwards, and a shard is just a stack of these consulted together.

options.t: A shard replica living on another node
options.why: Replicas are copies of a whole shard across machines. Segments live inside a single shard.

options.t: The portion of a posting list that fits in one disk block
options.why: Posting lists are stored in blocks, but a segment is a whole self-contained index — term dictionary, postings, doc values and all.

options.t: A cached query result set
options.why: Segments are on-disk index structures, not caches of answers.

items.q: What happens when you delete a document from a search index?

options.t: Its entries are removed from every posting list immediately
options.why: That would mean rewriting roughly a hundred compressed, sorted lists per delete — the exact cost immutability exists to avoid.

options.t: The segment containing it is deleted
options.why: That would drop thousands of unrelated live documents. Only the merge process rewrites segments, and it copies the survivors.

options.t: A bit flips in a tombstone bitmap until the next merge
options.why: Right. The document is marked not-alive and filtered at query time, still occupying disk until a merge rewrites the segment without it. An update is a delete plus an insert.

options.t: It is moved to a tombstone segment
options.why: No data is moved. The deletion is recorded as a bit in a per-segment liveness mask.

items.q: Why is search described as 'near-real-time' rather than real-time?

options.t: Because network latency between shards adds delay
options.why: Fan-out costs milliseconds, not seconds. The freshness delay comes from indexing, not query networking.

options.t: Because new documents only become visible at the next refresh
options.why: Documents sit in an in-memory buffer until the refresh interval (a second by default) freezes them into a segment. Freshness is quantized by design — that's the 'near'.

options.t: Because replicas are eventually consistent with the primary shard
options.why: Replica lag exists, but even the primary shard cannot show a document before the refresh that makes it searchable.

options.t: Because merges must complete before documents are visible
options.why: Merges are background housekeeping; a document is searchable as soon as its segment exists, long before any merge touches it.

items.q: Why do engines keep a column-oriented 'doc values' structure alongside the inverted index?

options.t: To store the original document text shown in results
options.why: That's stored fields, a separate thing fetched only for the handful of winners. Doc values are for computing over many documents.

options.t: To speed up term lookups
options.why: Term lookups already go through the term dictionary and postings. Doc values answer the opposite question.

options.t: Sorting and faceting need per-document field values
options.why: The inverted index says which docs contain X; it can't cheaply say what category each of 40,000 matching docs has. A packed per-field column makes 'walk the matches, tally the ordinals' fast.

options.t: To store the tombstone bitmaps
options.why: Liveness bitmaps are their own small per-segment structure and are unrelated to columnar field storage.

items.q: You estimate a 250 GB index, 12 shards, and 10,000 queries/sec. Your first design does 12 ms of CPU work per shard-query. What does that number tell you?

options.t: Nothing much — 12 ms sits comfortably inside a 200 ms p99 budget
options.why: The latency fits, but the cost doesn't. Fan-out multiplies work: latency budget and CPU budget are different constraints and this one blows the second.

options.t: You should add more replicas
options.why: Replicas do add read throughput, but you'd be buying hardware to serve work that shouldn't exist. Cut the per-query cost first, then size the fleet.

options.t: You should reduce the shard count to 4 to cut fan-out
options.why: Fewer shards means bigger shards doing more work each, so total CPU barely moves while merges and recovery get worse. The per-shard cost is the real lever.

options.t: ~1,400 cores of query CPU — per-shard work is the lever
options.why: 10,000 QPS times 12 shards is 120,000 shard-queries/sec; at 12 ms each that's ~1,440 CPU-seconds per second. At this fan-out every extra millisecond costs about 120 cores, which is why skip pointers and a cheap first-pass scorer are architecture, not trivia.

items.q: Merchandising wants to edit the synonym list weekly based on search logs. A full reindex of your 500M documents takes about 3 hours. Where do you apply synonyms?

options.t: At query time, expanding the incoming query
options.why: The list becomes a config change that takes effect in seconds. You pay a slightly wider query at runtime, and multi-word synonyms need care — a fair price for decoupling a weekly decision from a 3-hour job.

options.t: At index time, so queries stay fast
options.why: It is faster at query time, but every weekly edit now costs a 3-hour rebuild and skews term statistics. You've tied a routine business change to a heavyweight operation.

options.t: Both, for maximum recall
options.why: Doubling up multiplies the index bloat and the query width while making relevance harder to reason about — you can no longer tell where a match came from.

options.t: Neither; train the ranking model to learn synonyms instead
options.why: A reranker can only reorder what retrieval found. If 'sneakers' never matches a listing saying 'trainers', no model downstream can rescue it.

items.q: Your index stores doc IDs and term frequencies. Product now wants quoted phrase search. What must change?

options.t: Nothing — just AND the terms and check the order in the results
options.why: You can't check order without knowing where each term appeared. Postings as described don't record positions at all.

options.t: Store term positions, then verify adjacency
options.why: Postings gain the offsets where each term occurs; you intersect as usual, then walk position lists to keep only docs where the words are adjacent in order. Cost: positions roughly double or triple index size, and it's why you can't strip stopwords if phrases matter.

options.t: Switch from BM25 to a phrase-aware scoring function
options.why: Scoring is downstream of matching. No scorer can find phrases if the index doesn't record where terms sit.

options.t: Index every two-word pair as its own term
options.why: Indexing word pairs as terms (shingles) does exist and can help specific phrases, but as a general solution the vocabulary explodes and arbitrary-length phrases still don't work. Positions are the standard answer.

items.q: A pricing engine will rewrite the price on every listing every 10 minutes. Where should price live?

options.t: In the indexed document, so filters and sorts are fast
options.why: Each rewrite is a delete plus an insert, so the index fills with tombstoned documents and merges must continuously rewrite the whole thing. This is how a cluster enters a merge death spiral.

options.t: In the index, but with the refresh interval raised to 5 minutes
options.why: A longer refresh reduces segment churn slightly but does nothing about 500M deletes-plus-inserts per cycle, which is the actual problem.

options.t: In the index, with nightly full reindexing
options.why: Then prices are up to a day stale, which defeats the point of a pricing engine, and you still pay a 3-hour rebuild every night.

options.t: Outside the index, applied at rerank time
options.why: Churn rate decides membership in a read-optimized structure. Index the stable fields, keep the volatile number outside, and if you must filter during retrieval index a rarely-changing bucket like 'under 5k' instead.

items.q: Segment count per shard has been climbing steadily for six hours. Query latency looks normal so far. What is happening?

options.t: Merges are losing to indexing; queries degrade next
options.why: Every query consults every segment, so a rising count is borrowed time. This is the best early-warning signal in a search cluster: it moves hours before latency alerts fire.

options.t: The refresh interval is too long for this write volume
options.why: A longer refresh creates fewer, larger segments. Rising counts point the other way — segments arriving faster than merges retire them.

options.t: Replicas are out of sync with the primary
options.why: Replica divergence shows up as inconsistent results or recovery traffic, not as a steady one-way climb in segment count.

options.t: Nothing to act on until p99 moves
options.why: Waiting for the symptom is exactly the on-call mistake this metric exists to prevent. By the time p99 moves, the merge backlog is hours deep.

items.q: A partner integration pages through results with from=100000, size=10. Why does this hurt?

options.t: The posting lists have to be re-read from disk each page
options.why: Posting lists are cached and re-scanned cheaply. The cost is in the merge, not the disk reads.

options.t: BM25 scores drift for low-ranked documents
options.why: Scores are computed identically regardless of rank position. The problem is the volume of candidates the merge must handle.

options.t: Deep pages miss recently indexed documents
options.why: Freshness is governed by the refresh interval and applies to every page equally.

options.t: Every shard must return its own top 100,010
options.why: No shard knows whether it holds global result #100,004, so all twelve ship their top 100,010 and the coordinator merges 1.2 million entries for ten results. Cap the page depth and give partners a cursor API instead.

items.q: How should changes get from Postgres into the search index?

options.t: CDC tails the replication log into a queue
options.why: The database's own commit log is the event source, so nothing committed is missed, the queue absorbs bursts, and a dead indexer resumes where it stopped. It also makes replay the standard recovery move.

options.t: The app writes to Postgres and then writes to the search cluster
options.why: Dual writes have no shared transaction: a crash or a timeout between them leaves the copies disagreeing silently and permanently, with no record of the drift.

options.t: A cron job reindexes rows changed in the last hour
options.why: Polling by timestamp misses clock-skew edge cases and deletes entirely, and an hour of lag fails the five-second freshness requirement.

options.t: Write to search first, then asynchronously to Postgres
options.why: That makes the derived index the front door for durability — the one job a search engine is not built for.

items.q: A teammate proposes stripping stopwords ('the', 'a', 'of') to shrink the index. Your response?

options.t: Agree — it cuts index size meaningfully
options.why: It does shrink things, but storage is not the binding constraint here, and you'd be trading a real feature for a small saving.

options.t: Strip them at index time but keep them at query time
options.why: Query and index analysis must match. Terms removed at index time simply cannot be matched later, whatever the query does.

options.t: Keep them, because removing them would break BM25's math
options.why: BM25 works fine on any vocabulary. The real reasons are phrase matching and the fact that IDF handles the weighting for free.

options.t: Keep them; phrase queries need them
options.why: 'The Who' and 'to be or not to be' break without stopwords and their positions, and BM25 gives near-zero weight to terms that appear everywhere. Deleting them hand-optimizes something the scorer already handles.

items.q: Your reranking model costs 300 microseconds per document. Where does it belong?

options.t: In retrieval, replacing BM25 as the scoring function
options.why: At 300 microseconds it would take minutes to score millions of matching documents. Retrieval must stay a few arithmetic operations per candidate.

options.t: On the final 10 results before display
options.why: Reranking only 10 documents can reorder them but cannot pull a better result up from position 200, which is where most of the gain lives.

options.t: In a nightly batch that precomputes scores per document
options.why: Relevance depends on the query, so a per-document precomputed score cannot capture it. Query-independent signals can be precomputed as features, but the model still runs at query time.

options.t: On the top ~1,000 candidates BM25 returns
options.why: That's the two-phase shape: cheap scoring over millions, expensive scoring over a thousand — a few milliseconds total. It's the slot every ranking model plugs into without touching retrieval.

items.q: The interviewer says: 'The index is keyed by term, so why not shard by term?' Which answer reads senior?

options.t: 'Both work; term-sharding is better for single-word queries, doc-sharding for multi-word ones. It depends on the workload.'
options.why: Option-listing under a direct challenge reads as no judgment. There is a decisive quantitative argument here and the interviewer is waiting for it.

options.t: 'I shard by document — term-sharding ships 8-million-entry lists across the network per query.'
options.why: Committed, with the number that kills the alternative and the failure-mode contrast. Doc-sharded queries stay local and degrade gracefully; term-sharded ones need terabits of internal bandwidth and break specific words entirely.

options.t: 'Term-sharding causes hot shards, so I'd add consistent hashing to spread the terms.'
options.why: It spots one real problem and then patches it while missing the fatal one: no hashing scheme avoids moving whole posting lists between machines to intersect them.

options.t: 'Elasticsearch shards by document, so I'd follow that.'
options.why: Appealing to what a tool does, without the reason, is exactly the answer the probe was designed to expose.

items.q: You have ten minutes of deep-dive time. Which topic is the crux of this problem?

options.t: Choosing between BM25 and classic TF-IDF scoring
options.why: Worth thirty seconds and a committed choice, but it's a well-understood default with no architectural tension behind it.

options.t: The API contract and pagination parameters
options.why: Necessary plumbing, and it should be quick. Spending deep-dive time here reads as avoiding the hard part.

options.t: Keeping an immutable index fresh in real time
options.why: That's the fire. Posting lists are fast because they're sorted, compressed and contiguous, which makes in-place updates impossible at 5,000 docs/sec — and segments, refresh intervals, merges and tombstones are all consequences of resolving it.

options.t: Which cloud provider hosts the cluster
options.why: An operational detail with no bearing on the design's hard problem.

items.q: You route documents by hash(seller_id) so each seller's catalog lives on one shard. What is the subtle danger?

options.t: Queries filtered to a single seller get slower
options.why: Those get faster — a single-seller query now hits one shard instead of twelve. The damage is elsewhere.

options.t: Per-shard term statistics diverge
options.why: Each shard computes IDF from its own documents, which only works when routing is random. An electronics shard thinks 'battery' is common while a shoe shard thinks it's rare, so the coordinator merges scores that aren't comparable — wrong rankings, with no error anywhere.

options.t: Deletes stop working correctly
options.why: Deletes are per-segment tombstones and are unaffected by which shard a document lives on.

options.t: Phrase queries break across shard boundaries
options.why: Each shard holds complete documents, so phrase matching is always local. Documents are never split across shards.

items.q: One shard of twelve has no live replica during a query. What do you return, and how do you justify it?

options.t: Fail the query with a 503 in every case — partial results are lies
options.why: Honest, but applied blindly it destroys a marketplace's revenue for a fault the user could not perceive. The point is that this is a per-product decision, not a universal rule.

options.t: Return partial results silently; users won't notice 8% missing
options.why: The commitment isn't wrong for this product, but hiding it is. Unflagged degradation means nobody pages, nobody investigates, and the outage becomes permanent.

options.t: Commit per product: flagged partials here, fail loudly elsewhere
options.why: Same mechanism, two justified answers. An empty page loses a sale and search is already approximate; but for e-discovery, 'no results' and 'we skipped 8% of the corpus' are different answers and only one is honest. The flag, log and alert are mandatory either way.

options.t: Retry the query until the shard recovers
options.why: Retrying against a shard with no live copy just burns the latency budget and adds load during an incident.

items.q: You need to change the tokenizer on a live 500M-document index. What's the plan?

options.t: Update the mapping and let new documents use the new analyzer
options.why: Now old segments hold terms produced by the old analyzer and new ones don't. Queries match inconsistently, nothing errors, and relevance rots silently — the worst failure mode in search.

options.t: Reindex in place, document by document, over a few days
options.why: You get the same mixed-analyzer index for days, plus 500M deletes-and-inserts churning merges on the live serving cluster.

options.t: New index, dual-feed, shadow-compare, flip the alias
options.why: The derived-store payoff and Part 2.11 verbatim. Truth is in Postgres, so a 3-hour rebuild is always available; the alias flip makes the cutover atomic and the old index makes the rollback instant.

options.t: Restore from last night's snapshot with the new mapping applied
options.why: Snapshots carry the segments as they were, terms and all. Changing tokenization requires re-analyzing the source text, which only a reindex does.

items.q: Corpus grows 10x to 5 billion documents and traffic to 100K QPS. What breaks first?

options.t: The inverted index structure itself stops scaling
options.why: It doesn't — postings compress and skip just as well at 5B documents. Blaming the data structure misses where the real pressure lands.

options.t: BM25 becomes too slow to compute
options.why: Per-candidate scoring cost is unchanged by corpus size; you touch more postings, but the scorer is the same handful of operations.

options.t: Fan-out: p99 becomes the worst of ~120 shards
options.why: Tail latency compounds with fan-out, so p99 becomes roughly the shards' p99.9 and one merging node hurts every query. The fixes are routing (locale or category in the shard key so a query touches a subset) and hedged requests.

options.t: The CDC pipeline runs out of ordering guarantees
options.why: Per-key ordering from the log survives scaling fine and is a throughput problem at worst — not the first thing that bends.

items.q: Relevance ships a strong new reranker but offline metrics barely move on tail queries. What do you suspect first?

options.t: The model is undertrained on tail queries
options.why: Possible, and easy to test — but it assumes the candidates were there to reorder, which is the assumption worth checking first.

options.t: Phase 1 never retrieved those documents
options.why: The recall ceiling. If BM25 misses the listing because the user typed 'sneakers' and the listing says 'trainers', no reranker can save it. Measure phase-1 recall at 1,000 before blaming the model — and this is exactly where a semantic retriever earns its place alongside the lexical one.

options.t: BM25 parameters need tuning
options.why: Tuning changes the order of retrieved candidates more than the set, so it rarely fixes documents that were never retrieved at all.

options.t: The index is stale on tail documents
options.why: Freshness applies uniformly by refresh interval; it doesn't selectively affect the tail of the query distribution.

items.q: You propose relaxing the search cluster's write-ahead-log fsync from per-request to per-batch. Is that defensible?

options.t: No — losing acknowledged writes is never acceptable
options.why: True for a system of record. This index isn't one, and applying primary-store rules to a derived store means paying for durability you already bought elsewhere.

options.t: Yes, because modern SSDs make fsync effectively free
options.why: The right conclusion from the wrong reasoning. If fsync were free there'd be nothing to gain; the argument has to be about where the truth lives.

options.t: Only if you also disable replicas to save the network round trip
options.why: Replicas provide availability and read throughput, not durability of last resort here. Dropping them trades away uptime for a saving you didn't need.

options.t: Yes — the index is derived; truth is in Postgres
options.why: This is the payoff of committing early that search is never authoritative. A crash costs a replay, not data — so you can buy real throughput with a trade that would be reckless in the primary store.
